messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# David Chen: A Prosecutor's Reckoning

David Chen was thirty-three years old when the Boston Marathon bombing happened. He was there that afternoon in April not as a prosecutor—his career was still three years away—but as a volunteer with the medical response team, stationed near the finish line to provide first aid support for runners. He had been bored mostly, checking his phone, thinking about dinner plans with his wife Sarah, when the first explosion detonated so close that the sound didn't register as sound at all but as a physical rupture in the air. His ears rang. People screamed. The second blast came seconds later, and in the chaos that followed, David moved toward the noise instead of away—a reflex born of training—but almost immediately he felt helpless. The injuries were catastrophic. He applied tourniquets with hands that shook. He held a woman's hand while she bled through the gauze he'd wrapped around her leg. He told people help was coming. He was not a trauma surgeon. He was a volunteer with a certification that suddenly meant nothing. When the professionals arrived, they moved him out of the way. He stood there, blood on his shirt, watching trained people do what he could not.

In the years that followed, David threw himself into law. He went to law school with a clarity of purpose that surprised even him—he would prosecute terrorism, would use the legal system to ensure that what happened that day meant something, that justice was served. He was good at his work. Meticulous. Unforgiving of detail. He made partner early. Sarah was proud of him, though she sometimes asked if he was sleeping, if he was okay. He said he was fine.

By his thirty-third year, the fine had become a fiction he no longer quite believed. The exhaustion was the first thing that stopped being manageable. David would come home from the office drained in a way that sleep didn't repair. It was a heaviness that lived in his chest, a depletion that made even walking up the stairs feel like moving through water. On the nights when fatigue overwhelmed him, the memories would come with a particular intensity—not as something he recalled but as something happening to him in real time. He would be lying in bed and suddenly he was there again, the sound of the blast so immediate, so present, that his body would jolt awake in terror. The memory didn't feel like a story he could tell. It was fragments: the woman's face, the smell of blood and smoke, the specific uselessness of his hands. He couldn't arrange these pieces into a coherent narrative, even in his own mind. When Sarah asked what was wrong, what he was dreaming about, he found he couldn't explain it.

Then came the night when his colleague David Morales brought a bottle of whiskey to celebrate a conviction. The smell of it—that particular sharp, acrid alcohol smell—sent David Chen into a panic so acute that he had to excuse himself to the bathroom. His heart was racing. The smell had transported him backward so completely that for several minutes he couldn't remember where he was. Later, he realized the smell matched something from that day, something in the wreckage that his mind had catalogued and filed away without his knowing.

Fireworks became impossible. The sound of a car backfiring on the street outside his office made him flinch visibly enough that his paralegal asked if he was alright. He began avoiding situations where loud noises might occur. He stopped going to baseball games with Sarah. He found reasons not to attend Fourth of July celebrations. These small retreats felt necessary, protective—ways of keeping the memories at bay.

But the weight of what he hadn't done that day never lifted. He had been there, trained and present, and yet people had suffered injuries he couldn't prevent. He had failed to protect them. This thought, once acknowledged, became a kind of constant companion. It expanded to other domains: he began to believe that people around him—colleagues, friends, even Sarah—were not what they appeared to be. How could he trust anyone's motives when he had so thoroughly failed to read the moment, to act decisively when it mattered? The guilt was not something he could prosecute away. No conviction brought relief.

Sarah finally insisted he see someone when she found him one morning sitting in the garage with the car running, unable to articulate why he was there. He had no plan, exactly, but he was tired—so very tired—and the thought of another day felt impossible. That was when David made the appointment. He came to his first session asking if there was any way to stop feeling like the bombing was still happening, if there was any way to forgive himself for being alive when others were not.
